title: Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen
seal: An argument one of you will write
reading: In eight years, three authors — one of them seated at this table — will publish four pages in the Physical Review under the title 'Can Quantum-Mechanical Description of Physical Reality Be Considered Complete?'. Take two particles that have interacted and then flown far apart. Measure the position of the first, and you can predict with certainty the position of the second; measure instead its momentum, and you can predict the second's momentum. The authors propose a criterion: if, without in any way disturbing a system, we can predict a quantity with certainty, there is an element of reality corresponding to it. Since the measurement on the first particle cannot disturb the distant second, the second must possess both a definite position and a definite momentum. The theory cannot assign both. Therefore, they conclude, the quantum description is incomplete.
detail: The state considered is a joint wave function for two particles with definite total momentum and definite separation. In the later version by Bohm (1951) the same logic is applied to two spin-½ particles in a singlet state, which is the form Bell used. The paper was drafted by Podolsky; Einstein wrote to Schrödinger that the essential point had been 'smothered by formalism' and preferred to put it as a choice: either the description is incomplete, or the real states of spatially separated systems are not independent.

claim.label: Separateness or completeness
claim.summary: The 1927 Einstein recognises his own later argument. The framing as a choice between completeness and separability is documented from Einstein's 1935 letters; its presentation to the 1927 Einstein is inference.
voice: I recognise this. Its heart is simple: if what I do here cannot change what is over there, then what is over there was already settled. I would not put it with so much apparatus. I would say plainly that the theory cannot be complete and at the same time respect the independent existence of distant things. One of the two must go, and I know which I would keep.
This is my screen example made sharper. The wave of two particles, far apart, and a choice made at one end. I wish I had seen it this clearly this week.
claim.reasoning: Separability of spatially distant systems plus perfect correlations implies pre-existing values the theory does not represent.

historical.note: Einstein co-authored the paper and, in a letter to Schrödinger of 19 June 1935, said the main point had been smothered by formalism. He restated the argument in terms of separability in 1948.

claim.label: An ambiguity in 'without disturbing'
claim.summary: Bohr's 1935 reply: there is no mechanical disturbance of the second system, but the choice of measurement on the first influences the very conditions that define the possible types of prediction about the second.
voice: The argument is elegant, but it hides an ambiguity in the words 'without in any way disturbing'. There is no mechanical disturbance of the second particle — agreed. But the choice of what we measure on the first changes the very conditions that define which kinds of prediction about the second are possible. Position and momentum predictions require mutually exclusive arrangements. The argument does not show incompleteness. It shows again why complementarity is needed.
claim.reasoning: 'Elements of reality' cannot be assigned independently of the experimental arrangement.

historical.note: Bohr's reply appeared in the Physical Review in October 1935 under the same title. He later called its phrasing 'inefficient'.

claim.label: The characteristic trait
claim.summary: Schrödinger responded to EPR by identifying the non-separable joint state — which he named entanglement — as the characteristic trait of quantum mechanics.
voice: This is exactly what troubles me. After they have interacted, the two particles are described by one wave that cannot be split into a wave for each. Our knowledge of the whole can be complete while our knowledge of the parts is not. I would call that not one trait of the theory, but the characteristic one.
claim.reasoning: A maximal description of a whole need not contain maximal descriptions of its parts.

historical.note: Schrödinger wrote to Einstein enthusiastically in June 1935 and published two papers that year, coining 'Verschränkung' and 'entanglement'.

claim.label: A wish written into a premise
claim.summary: Pauli regarded the EPR paper as a public mistake by Einstein. The argument attributed here — that separability is exactly what the theory denies — is inference from his letters.
voice: The argument assumes that each particle has its own separate reality after they have interacted. That assumption is precisely what the theory denies. Einstein has written his wish into a premise and then found it again in the conclusion.
claim.reasoning: The separability premise begs the question against quantum mechanics.

historical.note: Pauli wrote to Heisenberg in June 1935 that Einstein had once again spoken publicly on quantum mechanics, 'which is a catastrophe every time it happens', and urged a reply.

claim.label: Knowledge changes, not the particle
claim.summary: Heisenberg drafted an unpublished reply in 1935. The simple framing here — the measurement changes our knowledge, not the distant particle — is inference from his 1927 views.
voice: Nothing travels. The measurement on the first particle changes what we know about the second — that is all the wave describes. To demand that the second particle carry both values in secret is to ask again for the classical path, which the theory has taught us to give up.
claim.reasoning: ψ as a representation of knowledge of possible observations.

historical.note: Heisenberg wrote an unpublished manuscript in 1935 replying to EPR, discussed by Bacciagaluppi and Crull.

claim.label: My wave lives in configuration space
claim.summary: Inference from the structure of de Broglie's 1927 theory: particles there have definite positions, supporting EPR's conclusion — but the guiding wave for two particles lives in configuration space, so one particle's motion may depend on the other's position.
voice: If particles have definite positions, as in my guiding-wave scheme, then Einstein's conclusion is natural. But I notice something uncomfortable. For two particles my wave lives in configuration space, and the motion of one may then depend on where the other is, however far away. I am not sure my theory helps the separateness Einstein wants.
claim.reasoning: In pilot-wave dynamics the velocity of each particle depends on the configuration of all.
claim.later: This is exactly the nonlocality Bell later identified in the de Broglie–Bohm theory.

claim.label: What changes over there?
claim.summary: An inferred Socratic question in Ehrenfest's documented style.
voice: Bohr — say it plainly for me. If nothing physical changes at the second particle, what is it that changes when we choose what to measure on the first? If the answer is 'the conditions of definition', where do those conditions live?
claim.reasoning: Pressing Bohr's reply for a plain statement.
